point: Studies agree DER flexibility needs TSO-DSO coordination and aggregators but split on whether balancing or intraday markets suit it best.
Villar et al. show that the uneven regulation and varied response of DERs, plus availability risk, block their entry into balancing markets.
Xu and Eid find the same balancing barriers plus imbalance risk for the balance responsible party, which explains why fast reserves came first.
Settlement schemes between aggregators and balance responsible parties are required before DERs can serve anything beyond very short-term balancing.
Using DER flexibility for system needs can create congestion locally, so TSO and DSO interests conflict and coordination mechanisms are required.
Newman and MacDougall argue DERs fit intraday markets better, since real-time markets leave aggregators too little lead time to schedule.
An aggregated EV fleet can respond to prices when it has hours rather than minutes, so real-time trading wastes its value.
IRENA and Garnier and Madlener also favour intraday trading, because more DERs would curb price spikes and intraday volatility pays better than day-ahead.
